title: When cheaper job adverts change the UK wage-pressure signal
summary: Michal Stelmach, James Kensett and Philip Schnattinger argue that the same number of vacancies per unemployed worker means something different in an economy where employers can keep adverts open cheaply. Some of the long rise in the UK vacancy-to-unemployment ratio reflects a rise in its equilibrium value. That does not explain away the surge after the pandemic. In Figure 5, actual vacancies rose well above the estimated equilibrium, then fell back as demand weakened. By the end of the sample, actual tightness was below the authors’ benchmark, suggesting some spare capacity. This is staff research about the interpretation of a pay-pressure indicator. The paper gives no Monetary Policy Committee forecast or interest-rate recommendation.

The authors divide UK recruitment advertising expenditure, deflated to 2025 prices, by the stock of vacancies. In Table 1 this measure falls from £1,070 in 2005 to £140 in 2024. Newspaper spending gave way to online recruitment, and posts stayed open longer. The estimated duration increased from approximately three weeks in the 1990s to over six weeks in recent years (Figure 3). Longer duration itself reduces spending per outstanding vacancy for a given fee per advert. The authors estimate it accounts for about a seventh of the fall between 2001–09 and the following period. They also show that employers’ median cost per hire, which covers more activities than advertising, fell between 2011 and 2024. The measures have different denominators and the survey widened its coverage in 2011.

To estimate equilibrium vacancies, the paper fits an error-correction model to quarterly data over 1982–2025, using productivity and the posting-cost measure. It then divides fitted vacancies by the Bank’s estimate of equilibrium unemployment. When observed tightness diverged from this benchmark, vacancies generally accounted for more of the gap than unemployment did (Appendix A.3). Appendix B finds the expected negative cost coefficient across specifications. Evidence for a stable long-run relationship is weaker in the sample ending in 2007, before the largest cost declines.

A separate search-and-matching model compares a print-intensive period through 2009 with the online period from 2010. Lower costs make an additional vacancy worth posting even when the prospect of filling it quickly is modest. Figure 6 illustrates the resulting movement along the calibrated relationship between vacancies and unemployment. Equilibrium vacancies per unemployed worker rise from 0.19 to 0.40. Those two endpoints reproduce the regime averages by construction. The more informative check is whether the quarterly observations within the two regimes lie around the same curve. Including the one-off cost of training a new hire weakens the model’s sensitivity to a change in posting costs.

An important caveat for investors is that spending per vacancy shares a denominator with the quantity the paper seeks to explain. Appendix D uses German survey data on advertising per skilled external hire and filling times as an independent check. It finds a substantial initial decline there, followed by a partial recovery after 2012, while the UK index continued down. The authors interpret the common transition as evidence for a structural change while treating short-run fluctuations in the UK measure with greater caution. A rates analyst using the paper would have grounds to reconsider a historical benchmark for vacancy pressure. Establishing how accurately that adjustment forecasts wages in real time requires a separate test.

questions.question: Does the adjusted tightness gap improve an investor’s real-time forecast of wage growth?
questions.detail: The authors estimate equilibrium tightness and interpret the recent negative gap as slack. They do not run an out-of-sample wage-forecast comparison. The result matters for how much weight a rates desk should assign a vacancy release relative to pay or underemployment data. Reconstruct the indicator using the vacancies, advertising expenditure and equilibrium unemployment estimates available at each release date and compare its pay-forecast errors with those from raw V/U.

questions.question: How much of a new movement in the posting-cost index reflects a genuine change in price?
questions.detail: The common UK and German decline during the print-to-digital transition supports the long-run interpretation. Their subsequent divergence and the UK ratio’s vacancy denominator make an individual quarterly movement harder to interpret. For a portfolio manager deciding whether a fall in vacancies signals weaker demand, seek UK platform prices, recruiter invoicing and vacancy-duration microdata. Use those independent price and quantity series to check earlier apparent shifts in the index.

questions.question: Which kinds of vacancies still predict near-term hiring and pay pressure?
questions.detail: The aggregate evidence allows firms to maintain speculative vacancies more cheaply. The paper leaves sectoral variation and recruiting effort for future work. A change concentrated in persistent, rarely filled listings would imply a different earnings and rates outlook from a broad decline in actively recruited positions. Examine matched employer data on posting dates, screening activity, eventual hires and wage offers, distinguishing industries and repeats of the same vacancy.

limitation: The equilibrium estimates depend on the cost proxy, the historical vacancy splice and the assumed equilibrium unemployment rate. The authors’ results end with their data sample and express their own views.
